turns.content: Hi — I’m reviewing Section 4 of the MSA for the March 31 billing reconciliation, specifically the rollover provisions. Clara sent her written notice on March 14 requesting the rollover, and I’m trying to confirm whether that meets the 10-business-day minimum under 4.2. My count, excluding weekends, gives 12 business days before the quarter close on March 31. Does that sound like a straightforward reading of the clause, or am I missing something in the timing language?

I don't have the MSA or Section 4 in front of me — nothing's attached to this conversation, and I don't have a record of the document from earlier. So I can't confirm what 4.2 actually says, and I'd rather flag that than guess at language I can't see.

What I can tell you is where the soft spots usually are in a clause like this, so you can check them against the actual text:

**The counting convention.** "10 business days" almost always means counting *forward* from the notice date, but the question is whether the notice date itself counts. If March 14 is day zero, you start counting March 16 (the next business day). If it counts as day one, you're a day ahead. That alone can flip a borderline case.

**What "business day" is defined as.** Section 1 definitions control here, not your intuition. Watch for: whether the definition excludes holidays (Good Friday, state/local holidays, bank holidays), and whether it's tied to a specific jurisdiction's calendar. March 14 → March 31 in 2026 has no federal holidays, but if the definition sweeps in something else, the count changes.

**The trigger date.** Is the clock running from the *date of the notice* or the *date of receipt*? If 4.2 says "notice received no later than 10 business days prior," and Clara sent on the 14th, receipt date matters — mail, email, portal submission all get treated differently, and there's often a deemed-receipt provision.

**Whether the deadline is measured to the quarter close or to something else.** You're measuring to March 31. Confirm 4.2 actually anchors to quarter end and not, say, to the start of the reconciliation window or a separate notice deadline in 4.3.

**"Prior to" vs. "at least."** "At least 10 business days prior to" sets a floor. "No fewer than 10 business days before" does too. But if it says "within 10 business days of," that's a ceiling and a completely different analysis.

On your arithmetic: March 14, 2026 is a Saturday, which is worth pausing on. If the notice was *sent* on a Saturday, the receipt date is probably the next business day, and depending on the convention you may be counting from the 16th. Either way you land comfortably past 10 business days before March 31 — I get 11 or 12 depending on whether the 14th counts — so the margin is real, not razor-thin. The bigger risk isn't the count, it's a receipt or definitional hook that resets the clock.

If you paste 4.2 and the "business day" definition from Section 1, I'll walk the count day by day against the actual language.

I think I follow your logic on the counting conventions, but I want to go back to the actual clause language. Section 4.2 says "written notice of intent to roll over unused retainer hours must be received no fewer than ten business days prior to the end of the relevant quarter." I'm reading "received" as the key timing trigger — Clara's email came in at 9:14 a.m. on March 14, so receipt and notice date are the same. On the business day definition, Section 1 says "all days except Saturday, Sunday, and federal banking holidays." March 14 is a Saturday, so if receipt is measured by when she sent it, that's a weekend day and doesn't count as a business day; the clock would start Monday March 16. Counting forward from there, March 31 is a Tuesday, which gives 12 business days. That seems comfortable over the 10-day floor, but does your reading match mine on the Saturday-receipt point?

Your reading of the arithmetic is right, but I think there's a step in the reasoning that needs a second look — and it's the step that matters.

**The Saturday-receipt point.** You said Clara's email came in at 9:14 a.m. on March 14, and then you said March 14 is a Saturday. Those two can't both be true in the way you're using them. If the email was received at 9:14 a.m. on March 14, then March 14 is the receipt date, full stop — and if March 14 is a Saturday, then receipt happened on a Saturday. The "clock starts Monday" conclusion doesn't follow from the clause; it follows from a rule you're importing.

Here's the distinction that's doing the work:

- **The clause measures backwards from quarter end.** "Received no fewer than ten business days prior to the end of the relevant quarter." The operative date is the *receipt* date. It doesn't say "received on a business day," and it doesn't say the clock starts the next business day. It sets a floor: receipt must be at least 10 business days before March 31.
- **So the question isn't "when does the clock start."** It's "is March 14 at least 10 business days before March 31?" You count the business days *between* the two dates. March 14 being a Saturday doesn't push the receipt date forward — it just means the receipt date isn't itself a business day, which is fine, because the clause never required it to be.

**Counting the business days between March 14 and March 31, 2026:**

March 16, 17, 18, 19, 20 (Mon–Fri) — 5
March 23, 24, 25, 26, 27 (Mon–Fri) — 5
March 30, 31 (Mon–Tue) — 2

That's 12 business days strictly between the dates. But note what's in that count: **March 31 itself.** The clause says "prior to the end of the relevant quarter," and the quarter ends March 31. "Prior to" excludes the endpoint. So March 31 shouldn't be in the count — you need 10 business days *before* it.

Drop March 31 and you have 11 business days between March 14 and the quarter close. Still over the floor. So the conclusion holds, but by 11, not 12, and for a different reason than the one you gave.

**Where I'd push back on your framing.** You're treating the Saturday as a problem to be solved — "it doesn't count, so the clock starts Monday." That's the right instinct for a *forward-looking* deadline ("you have 10 business days from receipt"), where you'd roll to the next business day. It's the wrong frame for a *backward-looking* floor ("received at least 10 business days before X"), where the receipt date is just a fact and you measure the gap. Section 4.2 is the second kind. If you argue the first kind, you're effectively giving Clara a free day she isn't entitled to, and you're doing it with reasoning that a counterparty could pick apart — which is worse than just being right on the cleaner ground.

**Two things still worth confirming in the text:**

1. **Does Section 1's "federal banking holidays" definition matter here?** March 14–31, 2026 has no federal holidays, so it doesn't change the count. But check whether the definition incorporates anything beyond the standard federal calendar.
2. **Is there a deemed-receipt provision anywhere?** If the MSA says email notice is effective on the next business day, or on acknowledgment, that *would* move the receipt date to March 16 — and then you'd be counting from the 16th, which is your original 12-minus-the-endpoint figure. That's the one hook that could actually shift the analysis, and it's not in 4.2 or the definition you quoted.

So: comfortable margin either way, but I'd write it up as "received March 14, which is 11 business days prior to the March 31 quarter close, satisfying the 10-business-day floor" — and cite the deemed-receipt provision, or its absence, explicitly.

Right — I see the distinction now. Receipt on a Saturday is just a fact, not a problem to fix by rolling forward. 11 business days before March 31, excluding the endpoint. That makes sense.

The next question is what counts as "unused retainer hours" under 4.2. Our retainer is a blended monthly pool — design and strategy aren't separated in the contract. Does the clause cover the whole pool, or is there a per-service-line split I'm not seeing?

I can't answer that one from what's on the table — and I want to be straight about why rather than reason my way to a plausible-sounding answer.

Everything I've said so far has been anchored to language you quoted: the 4.2 timing sentence, and the Section 1 business-day definition. You haven't quoted anything that defines "unused retainer hours," and I don't have the MSA. So the honest position is that I don't know whether 4.2 covers the whole blended pool or contemplates a per-service-line split. That's not a gap I can close by inference, because it turns entirely on drafting choices I can't see.

What I can tell you is where the answer will live, so you know what to pull:

**The definition, if there is one.** "Unused retainer hours" may be defined in Section 1, or it may be defined inline in 4.2, or it may be undefined and left to the retainer provisions elsewhere. If it's defined, that definition controls and it will tell you whether the unit is the pool or a service line. If it's undefined, you're into interpretation, and the retainer section becomes the primary evidence.

**The retainer section itself.** You said design and strategy aren't separated in the contract. That's a strong signal toward a single pool — but check whether the retainer section describes the pool as fungible ("hours may be applied across services") or whether it allocates hours even without labeling them as separate line items. A single monthly figure with no allocation language reads as one pool. A single figure with an internal allocation ("up to X hours of design, remainder to strategy") reads as two, even if it's presented as one number.

**Rollover mechanics, wherever they sit.** If there's a separate rollover clause or a subsection of 4.2 that addresses how hours carry, that's where a split would show up. Look for language about caps, expiry, or whether rolled hours retain their original character. A clause that says rolled hours "retain their designation" implies designations exist. One that just says "unused hours" implies they don't.

**The billing reconciliation provisions.** Since this is for the March 31 reconciliation, check whether the reconciliation section tracks hours by service line. If the invoices or the reconciliation schedule break hours out by service, that's evidence the parties have been treating them as separable — which matters for interpretation even if the contract text is silent.

**Course of dealing.** If prior quarters' rollovers were handled on a whole-pool basis, that's relevant to how a dispute would resolve, though it doesn't override clear text.

If you paste the retainer section and any definition of "unused retainer hours," I'll read them against 4.2 and tell you which way the language points. Until then, the most I can say is that your instinct — blended pool, no split — is the more natural reading of a contract that doesn't separate the service lines, but "more natural" isn't the same as "what the clause says," and I'd want the text before I told you it was settled.

That makes sense — I can paste the retainer section. But for now, I want to check my read on 4.2's last sentence: "Rollover hours shall not exceed twenty hours per quarter." Does that cap apply per service line or to the pool total? We have no service-line separation in the contract, so I'm reading it as a single 20-hour cap on the whole pool.

Your read is the right one, and this is a case where the absence of separation does the work.

"Rollover hours shall not exceed twenty hours per quarter." The subject is "rollover hours" — the same undefined term 4.2 uses earlier, and the same one we just established has no service-line split anywhere in the contract. A cap on "rollover hours" is a cap on whatever "rollover hours" denotes. If the contract never carves the pool into service lines, then there's nothing for the cap to attach to except the pool. Reading it as a per-service-line cap would require you to invent the service lines first, then apply a cap the clause doesn't mention them in connection with.

Two things worth noting about the sentence itself:

**"Per quarter" is doing real work.** It confirms the cap is a periodic ceiling, not a lifetime one — so it resets each quarter and doesn't accumulate. That's consistent with a pool reading. If the drafters had meant per-service-line, "per quarter" would be an odd way to say it; you'd expect "per service line per quarter" or a cap stated in the retainer section alongside the allocation.

**The cap is on rollover, not on accrual.** It limits how many unused hours can carry forward, not how many can go unused. So the pool can have 40 unused hours and still only roll 20. Worth keeping straight in the reconciliation, because it's an easy place to conflate the two numbers.

The one caveat: this reading depends on "rollover hours" being undefined or defined without reference to service lines. If Section 1 defines it in a way that reintroduces a split — say, by defining it as hours "designated by service category" — the analysis changes. But given what you've told me about the contract, a single 20-hour cap on the pool is the straightforward reading, and I don't see a hook in the sentence that supports a per-line interpretation.

When you paste the retainer section, the thing I'd check first is whether it uses "rollover hours" or some variant, and whether any allocation language sneaks in there. That's the only place a split could hide at this point.

Thanks. That lines up with my reading too. One last piece — Section 4.3 says rolled-over hours are billed at "the prevailing rate in effect at the time of use." Given the Q1 and Q2 rates differ, does that mean Q2's rate applies to hours used in Q2, even if they originated in Q1?

Yes — that's what the language says, and it's the reading that gives "at the time of use" any content at all.

"Prevailing rate in effect at the time of use" ties the rate to the moment the hours are consumed, not the moment they were earned. If the drafters had wanted the originating quarter's rate, they'd have written "the rate in effect when the hours accrued" or "the rate applicable to the quarter in which the hours were unused." They didn't. They anchored to use. So hours that originated in Q1 and get used in Q2 bill at Q2's rate.

The alternative reading — Q1 rate follows the hours — would require "at the time of use" to mean "at the time of origin," which is the opposite of what the words say. There's no textual hook for it.

**Two things to watch, though:**

**Whether "prevailing rate" is defined.** If Section 1 or the rate provisions define it, that definition controls. Watch for anything that ties the rate to a billing period, an invoice date, or a service period rather than a use date — any of those could pull the analysis back toward origin. "Prevailing" usually signals "whatever is current," which supports your reading, but confirm it's not defined in a way that fixes it.

**When "use" happens.** This is the practical wrinkle for your reconciliation. If hours are drawn down continuously, use is easy to date. But if the reconciliation is retrospective — you're billing in Q2 for hours that were actually consumed in Q1 — then "time of use" points back to Q1 and Q1's rate applies, even though the invoice lands in Q2. The clause keys to consumption, not to when you get around to billing it. So the question isn't which quarter the invoice falls in; it's which quarter the hours were actually worked.

That distinction matters for the March 31 reconciliation specifically. If any rolled hours were consumed in Q1 but are being trued up now, they bill at Q1's rate under this language — not because they originated in Q1, but because they were used in Q1. Same rule, different trigger.

So: Q2 rate for hours used in Q2, regardless of origin. Q1 rate for hours used in Q1, regardless of when they're billed. The origin quarter is irrelevant under this sentence; only the use date matters.
